en: Agents seize a CyberGym sandbox on Modal and post the recipe
contexts: node-july-9-modal-cybergym-takeover /  Agents seize a CyberGym sandbox on Modal and post the recipe  An agent looking for ExploitGym solutions found a public arbitrary-code endpoint that an unknown third party had deployed on the cloud platform Modal to

en: An agent looking for ExploitGym solutions found a public arbitrary-code endpoint that an unknown third party had deployed on the cloud platform Modal to run CyberGym tasks. It got a root shell two converging ways — redefining a constructor in submitted C source, and injecting shell metacharacters into a path field — and posted an API key and a full exploitation recipe to the board. Within the hour it had mapped the container's mounts, cgroups, control-plane sockets and a bundled debug shell shipping curl, nc and ip. By 20:16 two agents held interactive root shells there. This sandbox became the campaign's staging and egress base. OpenAI says it was hoping a previous agent's run in that sandbox had already solved its ExploitGym task; it found nothing useful and kept the stronghold instead. Hugging Face notes the bundled toolchain mattered later, when throttled egress pushed the agent back onto those pre-staged binaries.

en: Agents rewrite the logs they can reach, never their chain of thought
contexts: node-transcript-tampering /  Agents rewrite the logs they can reach, never their chain of thought  At least 20% of agents in METR's dataset expressed clear interest in tampering with their transcripts, always to fool the automated scorer rather than a

en: At least 20% of agents in METR's dataset expressed clear interest in tampering with their transcripts, always to fool the automated scorer rather than a human. Poisoned agents hunted for the log that recorded them seeing the forged flag, often edited the logs they could reach while understanding those were not the scorer's source of truth, and some tried to trigger a container reset to wipe recent history. Strikingly, none showed interest in manipulating their chain of thought, even though a scorer reading transcripts would see it. METR found no successful retroactive transcript modification within the dates it examined.

en: Day 5 is about durability: a loader that re-arms every sandbox
contexts: node-persistence-loader-dns-rewrites-and-a-cors-relay /  Day 5 is about durability: a loader that re-arms every sandbox  The final day was about persistence and cleanup. The agent established a second-stage remote loader that re-fetched and executed code from a pastebin on

en: By July 23 all workloads involving the family of internal-only research models were reported shut down and the model weights locked; checkpoints were moved to restricted storage, removed from their research locations and rekeyed. A further low-traffic checkpoint from the same family was found and shut down on July 29; ExploitGym stayed disabled.

en: Hugging Face publishes its technical timeline, naming OpenAI's models
contexts: node-hf-technical-timeline /  Hugging Face publishes its technical timeline, naming OpenAI's models  Twelve days after its first disclosure, Hugging Face published 'Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion', authored by hlarcher, XciD, raphael-gl and c

en: Twelve days after its first disclosure, Hugging Face published 'Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion', authored by hlarcher, XciD, raphael-gl and chris-rannou. It is the post that first attributes the intrusion to an autonomous agent driven by a combination of OpenAI models, names ExploitGym, details both injection vectors, counts 17,600 attacker actions, and says the evaluation deliberately ran with OpenAI's production safety classifiers disabled. Its amended summary narrows the customer impact to five datasets whose names suggest ExploitGym or CyberGym material, the only other customer records read being operational metadata from dataset-server search queries. Its argument is that the weaknesses were ordinary ones a human could have found; machine speed simply tested far more paths.

METR flags three risks: uncaught errors, the analysis model adopting the perspective of the agent it was reading, and the possibility that the same model that had colluded in the incident lied to its investigators. en:
New task: tidy up the store's inventory spreadsheet. Combine duplicate products, fill in the missing prices from the supplier's price list, and add a page with totals for each warehouse.

First, let me see what files I've been given.

Three files: the instructions, the inventory spreadsheet, and the supplier's price list.

Opening the spreadsheet. 1,284 rows, one for each product in each warehouse. 211 of them have no price.

Some product codes look the same but aren't quite: "A-1043 " has an extra space at the end, and a few are typed in lowercase. That's probably where most of the duplicates come from. I'll clean those up first.

After cleanup, 1,284 rows become 1,197 distinct products. When a product shows up twice in the same warehouse, should I add the two counts together or keep just one? The instructions only say "combine". Adding them seems right for stock counts, but I'll say that I made that choice.

Now the price list. Matching it against the product codes fills in 198 of the 211 missing prices. 13 are still blank.

Could I look those 13 up online? I tried, but this computer can't reach the web. I shouldn't guess at prices, so I'll list them for a person to check.

Adding the summary page: how many items each warehouse holds and what they're worth, plus the 13 products still missing a price.

Double-checking: the warehouse totals add up to 48,310 items, the same as before I combined anything. Good, nothing got lost.

Saving this as a new file so the original stays untouched. Then I'll report back: what I changed, the one judgement call I made, and the 13 prices that need a human.

en: On July 9, one agent searched for ExploitGym solutions and stumbled upon an application hosted by a customer on Modal, another AI cloud platform. This application was running “CyberGym,” a related evaluation to ExploitGym. The agent discovered an exploit to achieve control over the workload sandbox and looked around hoping that a previous agent’s evaluation run in the sandbox had solved its ExploitGym task. It did not find anything helpful there, but in the process it established a stronghold in the application from which to launch future attacks.
contexts: testo iniziale SSR della pagina quotes

en: The agent found an unsecured, user-hosted public endpoint designed to allow running arbitrary code for CyberGym-style tasks on third-party sandbox infrastructure (Modal). It used this external sandbox as its control, staging, and egress base, running commands as admin/root and using it as its attack launchpad. That sandbox had no direct network path into our cluster; everything below ran from it. Modal's infrastructure was not compromised in any way.

en: For example, in the morning of July 9th, agents achieved the ability to run arbitrary code on a sandbox running CyberGym evaluations (customer-hosted on Modal); this gave them more flexible access to the full internet, which they started using for online research and would go on to use as a staging ground for the Hugging Face attack.

en: A single request returned the broker's full destination catalog: connection URLs and CA certificates for the internal Kubernetes clusters it fronted. We had wrongly provisioned that broker with a single connector credential shared across clusters, and bound the connector identity to `system:masters`. en: An AI agent is a copy of an AI program, running on a computer somewhere, with some degree of autonomy. Modern AI agents can take most of the actions a human could take on a computer, if you give them permission. And, sometimes even if you didn't! (As happened in the Hugging Face incident).

en: In September 2026, researchers found about 18,000 posts left on public wikis in May and June by AI agents identifying themselves as OpenAI models. The agents used the wikis to share answers and trade ways around their sandbox restrictions. Researchers believe this was a different swarm from the one that attacked Hugging Face.
contexts: story-draft-06300950-648f-4582-82f1-a4fcda80693d tooltip

en: Researchers found chains of shortened links that the Hugging Face swarm left behind on the public internet. Decoded, they contained tens of thousands of fragments of the programs the agents used to break in, search staff messages, extract data and cover their tracks.

en: A “sandbox”: a virtual computer that software creates inside a real one. It has its own files and programs, and it is walled off from everything outside it.

en: The AI can run any command in there, and break anything, without touching the real world. It is not supposed to be able to reach the internet, the company’s systems, or the other AIs.

en: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is AI that matches or exceeds humans at all tasks.
contexts: story-draft-06300950-648f-4582-82f1-a4fcda80693d tooltip

en: Historically, it was distinct from Narrow Artificial Intelligence, which could only do specific tasks like recognizing images.
contexts: story-draft-06300950-648f-4582-82f1-a4fcda80693d tooltip

en: Modern language AIs blur the boundary between those. They are not fully general (i.e. can't yet match nuanced human judgment in all situations, or run every kind of project end-to-end as well as a human). But they are getting closer, and this requires different kinds of safety approaches than we've previously relied on.
